extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys and agents drafting U.S. patent specifications and claims
extracted.subtask_description: Practical drafting guidelines for U.S. patent specifications and claims distilled from Federal Circuit and Supreme Court decisions, with emphasis on avoiding common pitfalls (means-plus-function, indefiniteness, divided infringement, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid labeling anything as 'the invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to embodiments or examples rather than calling a particular disclosure 'the invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SciMed: If the specification describes a particular embodiment as 'the invention', courts may construe other claims to require that specific structure. Draft to present multiple embodiments and use neutral language like 'embodiments' or 'examples' rather than definitive phrases such as 'the invention.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Define unusual claim terms in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms receive their ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phillips: Do not rely on dictionaries alone to define terms. For unusual or nonstandard terminology, provide explicit definitions in the spec so the intended scope is clear to a POSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid functional/nonce language that invites 35 U.S.C. §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional language without adequate structural support can trigger means-plus-function treatment even if the word 'means' is not used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Williamson: Use specific structural language (e.g., 'processor,' 'circuit,' 'memory') rather than generic/nonce terms ('module,' 'mechanism,' 'unit') when you do not intend a means-plus-function construction. Provide structural detail in the spec to support claimed functional elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose algorithms for software-related means-plus-function elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming software functions under means-plus-function, the specification must disclose an algorithm (flowchart, pseudocode, or descriptive prose) that performs the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocrat: Do not rely on describing a 'general-purpose computer' alone. Include algorithmic disclosure (flowcharts, pseudocode, or clear prose describing the steps) to provide corresponding structure for software-implemented functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure definiteness — provide reasonable certainty for claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim language must be 'reasonably certain' to a POSITA in view of the specification and prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nautilus: For claim terms that are not standard in the field, the specification should give enough clarity and context so a POSITA can ascertain the bounds of the claim with reasonable certainty. Provide definitions, examples, and context for borderline or ambiguous terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft method claims to avoid divided infringement problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure method claims so a single actor performs every step or so that one actor directs or controls the actions of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Akamai: Because divided performance by multiple actors can defeat direct infringement, draft method claims carefully — either concentrate steps so a single actor necessarily performs them, or include claim language and factual support showing how a single actor directs/controls others (e.g., contractual or agency relationships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Address multiple failure modes for software patents separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Software claims face risks under 35 U.S.C. §101 (abstract idea), §112(b) (indefiniteness), and §112(f) (means-plus-function) — each must be addressed in the specification and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine defenses: disclose a concrete technical improvement to support §101; use structural language and corresponding structure to avoid §112(f); provide clear term definitions to satisfy §112(b); include algorithmic flowcharts and descriptions per Aristocrat to supply structure for software functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amend surgically and explain reasons to preserve doctrine-of-equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim amendments during prosecution can create a presumption that the amended element surrenders equivalents for that element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Festo: Because amendments can foreclose doctrine-of-equivalents reach, amend only as narrowly as necessary and record clear reasons for the amendment. If an amendment would not save the claim, consider cancelling the claim instead of making sweeping changes that could limit equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose numeric ranges and representative endpoints to support claimed ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims that will rely on numeric ranges, the specification must disclose the range or representative endpoints so the claim is supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Wertheim: When you might claim 'between 50 and 100', disclose multiple endpoints (e.g., 30, 50, 75, 100, 150) in the spec to ensure that claimed ranges have adequate written-description/support and to reduce vulnerability to challenges based on lack of range support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on asserted distinctions that are merely inherent in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed feature is inherent in a prior art reference, that prior art can anticipate the claim even if the feature is not expressly disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Kao: When distinguishing over prior art, rely on actively chosen and expressly disclosed features in the specification rather than features that might be inherent in the cited references. Provide explicit disclosure and argumentation distinguishing the claimed invention from inherent properties of the prior art.
